background.label: Malaria
background.definition: A protozoan disease caused in humans by four species of the PLASMODIUM genus: PLASMODIUM FALCIPARUM; PLASMODIUM VIVAX; PLASMODIUM OVALE; and PLASMODIUM MALARIAE; and transmitted by the bite of an infected female mosquito of the genus ANOPHELES. Malaria is endemic in parts of Asia, Africa, Central and South America, Oceania, and certain Caribbean islands. It is characterized by extreme exhaustion associated with paroxysms of high FEVER; SWEATING; shaking CHILLS; and ANEMIA. Malaria in ANIMALS is caused by other species of plasmodia.

background.label: Ivermectin
background.definition: A mixture of mostly avermectin H2B1a (RN 71827-03-7) with some avermectin H2B1b (RN 70209-81-3), which are macrolides from STREPTOMYCES avermitilis. It binds glutamate-gated chloride channel to cause increased permeability and hyperpolarization of nerve and muscle cells. It also interacts with other CHLORIDE CHANNELS. It is a broad spectrum antiparasitic that is active against microfilariae of ONCHOCERCA VOLVULUS but not the adult form.

claims.headline: JCAR017 was linked to remission of a brain lymphoma lesion in one trial participant
claims.summary: A Massachusetts General Hospital report described a patient with chemotherapy-resistant diffuse large B-cell lymphoma whose brain lesion went into complete remission after JCAR017 treatment. A later recurring skin lesion disappeared after biopsy without further treatment, alongside renewed expansion of the CAR T cells. The patient later relapsed and died, but the brain lesion did not return.

claims.headline: LSD-related compound JRT showed effects relevant to schizophrenia in mouse studies
claims.summary: UC Davis researchers developed JRT by changing the position of two atoms in LSD. In cellular and mouse tests, it promoted measures of brain plasticity and affected behaviors relevant to schizophrenia, while showing less hallucinogenic potential than LSD. The researchers say they are testing it in other disease models and developing additional versions.

background.label: Essential Tremor
background.definition: A relatively common disorder characterized by a fairly specific pattern of tremors which are most prominent in the upper extremities and neck, inducing titubations of the head. The tremor is usually mild, but when severe may be disabling. An autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance may occur in some families (i.e., familial tremor). (Mov Disord 1988;13(1):5-10)

claims.headline: Small study links liraglutide with fewer monthly migraine days
claims.summary: A 12-week study of 26 adults with obesity and frequent or chronic migraines found that average headache days fell from 20 to about nine after daily liraglutide. The article reports reduced migraine-related disability and mild side effects in about 40% of participants; researchers proposed that lower brain-fluid pressure may explain the result.

claims.headline: Lithium use for bipolar disorder has declined despite ongoing debate over its benefits and drawbacks
claims.summary: The article reports that lithium prescribing in the UK has fallen even as bipolar diagnoses rose. It describes evidence of lithium’s effectiveness, the monitoring and side-effect concerns that complicate its use, and proposals for research into predicting response and improving monitoring. One patient describes lithium as helpful in managing her condition.

background.label: Melanoma
background.definition: A malignant neoplasm derived from cells that are capable of forming melanin, which may occur in the skin of any part of the body, in the eye, or, rarely, in the mucous membranes of the genitalia, anus, oral cavity, or other sites. background.label: DRD1
background.name: dopamine receptor D1
background.definition: G protein-coupled receptor for dopamine, a catecholamine neurotransmitter hormone that functions as the brain's 'reward chemical', driving motivation, reinforcement learning and pleasure (PubMed:11500503, PubMed:33571431, PubMed:33571432, PubMed:33750903, PubMed:34083522, PubMed:35676276, PubMed:35687690, PubMed:37221270). Dopamine binding causes a conformation change that triggers signaling via guanine nucleotide-binding proteins (G proteins) and modulates the activity of downstream effectors, such as adenylate cyclase (PubMed:33571431, PubMed:33571432, PubMed:33750903, PubMed:34083522, PubMed:35676276, PubMed:35687690). Dopamine receptors can be classified in two categories: (1) DRD1 (together with DRD5) is a D1-type receptor and is coupled to G(s) G proteins, mediating activation of adenylate cyclase activity, while D2-type receptors (DRD2, DRD3 and DRD4) are coupled to G(i)/G(o) G proteins and promote inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity (PubMed:33571431, PubMed:33571432, PubMed:33750903, PubMed:34083522, PubMed:35676276, PubMed:35687690, PubMed:7782330). D1- and D2-type dopamine receptors have antagonistic effects, particularly in the brain's striatum, where they govern voluntary movement and reward: D1-type receptors generally stimulate neural activity and promotes action, while D2-type receptors tend to inhibit neural activity and suppress movement (By similarity). DRD1 acts as an essential regulator of reward, motor activity and cognition in the central nervous system and play beneficial roles in peripheral tissues including inhibiting inflammatory reactions and maintaining cardiovascular and kidney homeostasis (PubMed:33571431, PubMed:33571432). DRD1 and DRD2 are the most abundant dopamine receptors in the central nervous system, especially in the basal ganglia and the prefrontal cortex (PubMed:33571431, PubMed:33571432). DRD1 can also couple with G(q) by forming a heteromer with the ghrelin receptor GHSR in hippocampal neurons independently of ghrelin (By similarity). Following DRD1 activation by dopamine, GHSR acts as a coreceptor promoting DRD1 coupling to G(q) at the expense of G(s), initiating hippocampal synaptic plasticity involved in memory and learning (By similarity). Forms heterotetramers with DRD3 to potentiate beta-arrestin recruitment and mediate locomotor activity (By similarity). Also acts as a receptor for D-lysergic (LSD) psychedelic drug (PubMed:39094559). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:Q61616, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11500503, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33571431, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33571432, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33750903, ECO:0000269|PubMed:34083522, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35676276, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35687690, ECO:0000269|PubMed:37221270, ECO:0000269|PubMed:39094559, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7782330}.

background.label: Ischemic Stroke
background.definition: Stroke due to BRAIN ISCHEMIA resulting in interruption or reduction of blood flow to a part of the brain. When obstruction is due to a BLOOD CLOT formed within in a cerebral blood vessel it is a thrombotic stroke. When obstruction is formed elsewhere and moved to block a cerebral blood vessel (see CEREBRAL EMBOLISM) it is referred to as embolic stroke. Wake-up stroke refers to ischemic stroke occurring during sleep while cryptogenic stroke refers to ischemic stroke of unknown origin.

reported_statements.text: In the ferret study, no untreated cage-mates of treated source animals became infected, while all contacts of placebo-treated sources did.
reported_statements.speaker: researcher

reported_statements.text: Oral treatment of infected animals reduced the amount of virus they shed by several orders of magnitude.
reported_statements.speaker: researcher

reported_statements.text: It could give doctors another treatment for COVID-19 and a tool against coronaviruses and future pandemics.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: An early trial involving 202 participants found that molnupiravir rapidly lowered levels of infectious virus.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Antivirals may eventually be studied for preventing infection after exposure.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Among trial participants, hospitalization or death by 30 days occurred in 7.3% taking molnupiravir and 14.1% taking placebo.
reported_statements.speaker: company

reported_statements.text: No deaths occurred among drug recipients after the reported 30-day period, compared with eight in the placebo group.
reported_statements.speaker: company

reported_statements.text: Among high-risk adults with mild-to-moderate COVID-19, 7.3% taking molnupiravir were hospitalized or died within 30 days, versus 14.1% taking placebo.
reported_statements.speaker: company

reported_statements.text: The trial's early results indicated about half the rate of hospitalization or death when treatment began within five days of symptom onset.
reported_statements.speaker: company

reported_statements.text: Molnupiravir interferes with the virus copying its genetic code and reproducing.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Earlier study results found no benefit for patients already hospitalized with severe COVID-19.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: The regimen described was four pills twice daily for five days.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: No deaths occurred among participants given the treatment during the 29-day period, while eight deaths occurred in the placebo group.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: The treatment works by blocking coronavirus replication in the body.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Its effectiveness was reported as consistent across COVID-19 variants, including Delta, and unaffected by symptom timing or underlying risk factors.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Adverse events were reported by about 10% in both groups; 1.3% of treated participants and 3.4% of placebo participants stopped treatment because of an adverse event.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: If regulators authorize it, the treatment could become the first oral antiviral medicine for COVID-19.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: The tablet is designed to introduce errors into the virus’s genetic code and stop it spreading in the body.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: An earlier study in people already hospitalised with severe Covid was stopped after disappointing results.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: In an interim analysis, about 7.3% of recipients were hospitalized or died by day 29, compared with 14.1% of placebo recipients; no deaths occurred among recipients, versus eight with placebo.
reported_statements.speaker: company

reported_statements.text: If authorized, it would be the first oral antiviral treatment for COVID-19.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: It is authorised for mild-to-moderate COVID-19 in people with at least one risk factor for severe illness.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: The treatment needs to be started within five days of symptoms for the best effect.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: An earlier study in people already hospitalised with severe COVID-19 was stopped after disappointing results.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: It works by reducing the virus's ability to replicate, which slows the disease.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: It is authorized for people with at least one risk factor for severe illness, such as obesity, older age, diabetes or heart disease.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: It is described as relatively ineffective and dangerous.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: It might give rise to SARS-CoV-2 variants that evade immunity and prolong the pandemic.

claims.headline: Montelukast use is linked to reported mental health effects, with its brain action still unclear
claims.summary: The article reviews reports of psychiatric symptoms among people taking montelukast, including children, and research into the possible risks. A study of health records found modestly higher odds of insomnia diagnoses and antidepressant prescriptions after treatment; a mouse study suggested changes in brain chemicals. Researchers have not established how the drug reaches or affects the brain.

claims.headline: Brain-implanted visual prosthesis enabled a blind woman to perceive patterns and letters
claims.summary: A woman who had been blind for 16 years received the Moran|Cortivis Prosthesis, which stimulates the brain’s visual region. During six months of testing, she perceived light patterns, distinguished line orientations, identified some letters and used camera-equipped glasses to locate simple shapes. The article notes that the findings come from one participant and that longer, broader testing is needed.

articles.title: Brain Implant Gives Blind Woman Artificial Vision in Scientific First

background.label: Blindness
background.definition: The inability to see or the loss or absence of perception of visual stimuli. This condition may be the result of EYE DISEASES; OPTIC NERVE DISEASES; OPTIC CHIASM diseases; or BRAIN DISEASES affecting the VISUAL PATHWAYS or OCCIPITAL LOBE.

background.label: Prostheses and Implants
background.definition: Artificial substitutes for body parts, and materials inserted into tissue for functional, cosmetic, or therapeutic purposes. Prostheses can be functional, as in the case of artificial arms and legs, or cosmetic, as in the case of an artificial eye. Implants, all surgically inserted or grafted into the body, tend to be used therapeutically. IMPLANTS, EXPERIMENTAL is available for those used experimentally.

organisations.name: John A. Moran Eye Center at the University of Utah

reported_statements.text: Electrical stimulation produced perceived points of light, whose brightness and color varied with stimulation strength.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: By the end of training, the participant distinguished horizontal from vertical patterns with 100 percent accuracy.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: She identified several letters, including I, L, C, V and O, and distinguished uppercase O from lowercase o.

claims.headline: Study finds mouth guards may help treat obstructive sleep apnea
claims.summary: A report on 347 people fitted with mouth guards found that about two-thirds were comfortable wearing them, and the devices appeared to ease disordered breathing. The lead author described oral appliances as easier to tolerate and less costly than CPAP, and helpful for many people unable to use CPAP.

background.label: Sleep Apnea, Obstructive
background.definition: A disorder characterized by recurrent apneas during sleep despite persistent respiratory efforts. It is due to upper airway obstruction. The respiratory pauses may induce HYPERCAPNIA or HYPOXIA. Cardiac arrhythmias and elevation of systemic and pulmonary arterial pressures may occur. Frequent partial arousals occur throughout sleep, resulting in relative SLEEP DEPRIVATION and daytime tiredness. Associated conditions include OBESITY; ACROMEGALY; MYXEDEMA; micrognathia; MYOTONIC DYSTROPHY; adenotonsilar dystrophy; and NEUROMUSCULAR DISEASES. (From Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, p395)

background.label: Multiple Sclerosis
background.definition: An autoimmune disorder mainly affecting young adults and characterized by destruction of myelin in the central nervous system. Pathologic findings include multiple sharply demarcated areas of demyelination throughout the white matter of the central nervous system. Clinical manifestations include visual loss, extra-ocular movement disorders, paresthesias, loss of sensation, weakness, dysarthria, spasticity, ataxia, and bladder dysfunction. The usual pattern is one of recurrent attacks followed by partial recovery (see MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS, RELAPSING-REMITTING), but acute fulminating and chronic progressive forms (see MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS, CHRONIC PROGRESSIVE) also occur. claims.headline: Review finds nitrous oxide may provide rapid, short-term relief from depression
claims.summary: A review of seven clinical trials involving 247 participants found that inhaled nitrous oxide reduced depressive symptoms within two hours, though symptoms often returned within a week without another dose. claims.headline: Trial reports tumor responses with nivolumab and ipilimumab for advanced head and neck cancer
claims.summary: A phase 3 trial of nearly 1,000 patients found that nivolumab plus ipilimumab shrank tumors in some people with advanced head and neck cancer, with tumors becoming undetectable in some cases. Results were early and not statistically significant overall; patients whose tumors had high PD-L1 levels lived a median 17.6 months, about three months longer than those receiving chemotherapy.

background.label: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
background.definition: An anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent, persistent obsessions or compulsions. Obsessions are the intrusive ideas, thoughts, or images that are experienced as senseless or repugnant. Compulsions are repetitive and seemingly purposeful behavior which the individual generally recognizes as senseless and from which the individual does not derive pleasure although it may provide a release from tension.

background.label: Electric Stimulation Therapy
background.definition: Application of electric current in treatment without the generation of perceptible heat. It includes electric stimulation of nerves or muscles, passage of current into the body, or use of interrupted current of low intensity to raise the detection threshold of the skin to pain.

claims.headline: Survodutide was reported to reduce belly and liver fat in a Phase 3 obesity trial
claims.summary: The Mirror reported results from the Phase 3 SYNCHRONIZE-1 trial of survodutide, a once-weekly injection acting on glucagon and GLP-1 receptors. People with obesity but without type 2 diabetes lost up to 16.6 per cent of body weight over 76 weeks at the top dose, and a separate analysis found visceral fat down by up to 34 per cent and liver fat by up to 63.1 per cent. The article quotes a pharmacist saying the drug is still investigational and not approved, and notes the body-composition analysis involved a relatively small group.

claims.summary: The Daily Mail reported that University of California Berkeley researchers found the 1970s compound TOFA makes cells burn fat for energy, in a study in mice published in Science Advances. Obese mice lost about 8.7 per cent of body weight in 24 days on TOFA alone, and much more when it was combined with low doses of semaglutide or tirzepatide, with almost all the loss being fat. The article stresses TOFA has not yet been tested in humans, so its safety profile is unknown.

claims.headline: OpRegen study reports retinal tissue regrowth in some patients with dry AMD
claims.summary: A Phase I/IIa study reported retinal tissue regrowth and improved visual acuity in three patients with dry age-related macular degeneration and geographic atrophy. The article describes OpRegen as a one-time retinal cell transplant and reports benefits lasting up to three years in patients with available follow-up.

claims.headline: Light-based cochlear stimulation restored some auditory responses in deaf gerbils
claims.summary: A study used optogenetics to activate auditory neurons in gerbils with light. Deafened animals learned to respond to the stimulation, while brainstem responses remained stable for weeks. The approach could eventually improve hearing devices, but the study used only one optical channel and the article notes technical and gene-delivery challenges before human use.

claims.headline: Oral peanut immunotherapy reduced reactions to a measured peanut dose in a children’s trial
claims.summary: A yearlong trial tested gradually increased oral peanut-protein doses in children with severe peanut allergy. After treatment and maintenance, about two-thirds of treated children tolerated at least 600 milligrams of peanut protein without symptoms, compared with 4 percent receiving placebo. The article also reports withdrawals and adverse events, including epinephrine use.

background.label: Parkinson Disease
background.definition: A progressive, degenerative neurologic disease characterized by a TREMOR that is maximal at rest, retropulsion (i.e. a tendency to fall backwards), rigidity, stooped posture, slowness of voluntary movements, and a masklike facial expression. Pathologic features include loss of melanin containing neurons in the substantia nigra and other pigmented nuclei of the brainstem. LEWY BODIES are present in the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus but may also be found in a related condition (LEWY BODY DISEASE, DIFFUSE) characterized by dementia in combination with varying degrees of parkinsonism. (Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, p1059, pp1067-75)

claims.headline: Vitamin D supplements were associated with fewer suicide attempts and self-harm among US veterans
claims.summary: A retrospective study of 1.3 million US veterans found lower suicide-attempt and intentional-self-harm rates among those receiving oral vitamin D2 or D3 than among matched veterans without supplementation. Associations were stronger among Black veterans and people with low vitamin D levels, and increased with higher doses. The authors said clinical trials are needed to confirm the findings.

claims.headline: Eli Lilly reports trial results for daily orforglipron in people with Type 2 diabetes
claims.summary: Eli Lilly said a clinical trial found its daily pill orforglipron had blood-sugar and weight-loss results, and safety data, similar to injectable drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro. The company had not released detailed trial data; it said it would present results in June and seek regulatory approval for obesity later in 2025 and diabetes in early 2026.

reported_statements.text: Its pill form could make it more widely used than injectable GLP-1 drugs.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Over 40 weeks, average weight fell by 4.5% with 3 mg, 5.8% with 12 mg, and 7.6% with 36 mg daily.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: The company said the trial results met its expectations for safety, tolerability, blood-sugar control, and weight reduction.
reported_statements.speaker: company

reported_statements.text: If approved, it could offer a convenient treatment option and potentially be produced and launched at large scale.
reported_statements.speaker: company

reported_statements.text: Its effects on cardiovascular outcomes are not yet known, with further trials expected to address this.
reported_statements.speaker: other_expert

reported_statements.text: In the late-stage study, it lowered blood sugar and body weight, with safety described as comparable to popular injectable treatments.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: About 8% of people taking the highest dose stopped treatment because of side effects, which were mostly mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal symptoms.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: If approved, it could widen access to treatment and ease supply shortages of popular injectable medicines.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: As a once-daily pill, it could be manufactured and launched at scale for use around the world if approved.
reported_statements.speaker: company

reported_statements.text: How it compares with higher doses of oral semaglutide, particularly in people with overweight or obesity without diabetes, remains unclear.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: At 36 milligrams daily, participants lost an average of 9.6% of their body weight over 72 weeks.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Reported side effects included nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, and constipation, similar to those associated with injectable GLP-1 drugs.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Orforglipron activates the GLP-1 receptor and is absorbed through the digestive tract despite not being a peptide.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Its weight-loss result was lower than the 14.7% average reported for tirzepatide in an earlier trial of participants with diabetes.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: As an oral treatment, it could offer outcomes similar to injectable GLP-1 receptor agonists and potentially change treatment practices.
reported_statements.speaker: researcher

reported_statements.text: At 52 weeks, the 36-mg dose lowered a key blood sugar marker by nearly 2%, compared with nearly 1.5% for 14-mg oral semaglutide.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: The 36-mg dose led to average body-weight reduction of 8%, compared with 5% for 14-mg oral semaglutide.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Nausea, vomiting and other gastrointestinal effects, as well as treatment discontinuations, were more frequent than with semaglutide.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: It could help people with type 2 diabetes become less reliant on insulin.
reported_statements.speaker: other_expert

reported_statements.text: Participants had lower average blood sugar at the end of the trial than those taking either dose of oral semaglutide.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: It targets GLP-1 receptors, lowers blood sugar, slows digestion and suppresses appetite.
reported_statements.speaker: article

claims.headline: Osimertinib after surgery was linked to lower mortality in an EGFR-mutated lung cancer trial
claims.summary: In the Adaura trial, patients with EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer who took daily osimertinib after surgery had a 51% lower risk of death than those given placebo. Five-year survival was 88% with osimertinib and 78% with placebo. The article also reports earlier trial findings of reduced recurrence risk.

background.name: epidermal growth factor receptor
background.definition: Receptor tyrosine kinase binding ligands of the EGF family and activating several signaling cascades to convert extracellular cues into appropriate cellular responses (PubMed:10805725, PubMed:12297050, PubMed:12620237, PubMed:12873986, PubMed:15374980, PubMed:15590694, PubMed:17115032, PubMed:19560417, PubMed:21258366, PubMed:27153536, PubMed:2790960, PubMed:35538033, PubMed:9488479). Known ligands include EGF, TGFA/TGF-alpha, AREG, epigen/EPGN, BTC/betacellulin, epiregulin/EREG and HBEGF/heparin-binding EGF (PubMed:12297049, PubMed:15611079, PubMed:17909029, PubMed:20837704, PubMed:27153536, PubMed:2790960, PubMed:7679104, PubMed:8144591, PubMed:9419975). Ligand binding triggers receptor homo- and/or heterodimerization and autophosphorylation on key cytoplasmic residues (PubMed:10026169, PubMed:17349580, PubMed:18046415, PubMed:19560417, PubMed:19836242). The phosphorylated receptor recruits adapter proteins like GRB2 which in turn activates complex downstream signaling cascades (PubMed:10026169, PubMed:17349580, PubMed:18046415, PubMed:19560417, PubMed:19836242). Activates at least 4 major downstream signaling cascades including the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK, PI3 kinase-AKT, PLCgamma-PKC and STATs modules (PubMed:27153536). May also activate the NF-kappa-B signaling cascade (PubMed:11116146). Also directly phosphorylates other proteins like RGS16, activating its GTPase activity and probably coupling the EGF receptor signaling to the G protein-coupled receptor signaling (PubMed:11602604). Also phosphorylates MUC1 and increases its interaction with SRC and CTNNB1/beta-catenin (PubMed:11483589). Positively regulates cell migration via interaction with CCDC88A/GIV which retains EGFR at the cell membrane following ligand stimulation, promoting EGFR signaling which triggers cell migration (PubMed:20462955). Acts as a positive regulator of cGAS-STING signaling by mediating tyrosine phosphorylation of STING1, promoting production of type I interferon (IFN-alpha and IFN-beta), while inhibiting STING1 ability to regulate autophagy (PubMed:32926474). Plays a role in enhancing learning and memory performance (By similarity). Plays a role in mammalian pain signaling (long-lasting hypersensitivity) (By similarity). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:Q01279, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10026169, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10805725, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11116146, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11483589, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11602604, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12297049, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12297050, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12620237, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12873986, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15374980, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15590694, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15611079, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17115032, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17349580, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17909029, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18046415, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19560417, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19836242, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20462955, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20837704, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21258366, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27153536, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2790960, ECO:0000269|PubMed:32926474, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35538033, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7679104, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8144591, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9419975, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9488479}.

claims.headline: Removal of the fallopian tubes was reported as a way to lower the risk of ovarian cancer by up to 80 per cent
claims.summary: The Daily Mail reported that experts say removing the fallopian tubes could cut ovarian cancer risk by as much as 80 per cent, because most deadly ovarian cancers appear to start there. The procedure is already offered to high-risk women in a UK national research trial, and health bodies are encouraging doctors to offer it to women over 45 who are having other abdominal surgery. The article notes that 98 per cent of women will not develop ovarian cancer and calls the approach extreme.

background.label: Obesity
background.definition: A status with BODY WEIGHT that is grossly above the recommended standards, usually due to accumulation of excess FATS in the body. The standards may vary with age, sex, genetic or cultural background. In the BODY MASS INDEX, a BMI greater than 30.0 kg/m2 is considered obese, and a BMI greater than 40.0 kg/m2 is considered morbidly obese (MORBID OBESITY).

background.label: Oxytocin
background.definition: A nonapeptide hormone released from the neurohypophysis (PITUITARY GLAND, POSTERIOR). It differs from VASOPRESSIN by two amino acids at residues 3 and 8. Oxytocin acts on SMOOTH MUSCLE CELLS, such as causing UTERINE CONTRACTIONS and MILK EJECTION.

background.label: OXTR
background.name: oxytocin receptor
background.definition: G protein-coupled receptor for oxytocin (OXT), a neuropeptide hormone released by the posterior pituitary gland that plays a key role in social behavior and other biological processes, such as milk ejection (PubMed:11923477, PubMed:22069312, PubMed:32832646, PubMed:35104164, PubMed:35241813, PubMed:35851571). Ligand binding causes a conformation change that triggers signaling via guanine nucleotide-binding proteins (G proteins) and modulates the activity of downstream effectors, such as phospholipase C (PubMed:22069312, PubMed:32832646, PubMed:35104164, PubMed:35241813, PubMed:35851571). OXTR is mainly coupled to G(q) G proteins and mediates production of diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) second messengers that modulate the activity of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase and promote the release of Ca(2+) ions from intracellular stores, respectively (PubMed:11923477, PubMed:22069312, PubMed:32832646, PubMed:35104164, PubMed:35241813, PubMed:35851571). In presence of high levels of oxytocin, also coupled to G(i) G proteins, mediating inhibition of adenylate cyclase activity (PubMed:22069312, PubMed:35241813, PubMed:35851571). Central release of oxytocin plays essential roles in social behavior, such as maternal care, social cognition and affiliative behaviors, triggering signaling that modulates neural circuits by altering ion channel activity, changing intrinsic neuronal properties and modifying synaptic transmission (both excitatory and inhibitory) (PubMed:19934046, PubMed:20647384, PubMed:21896752, PubMed:22123970, PubMed:24367110). Peripheral release of oxytocin (secretion into the bloodstream) promotes various processes, such as parturition, lactation or osteoblast differentiation (PubMed:6278592). OXTR-mediated signaling promotes milk ejection by triggering and strengthening contraction of the smooth muscle of mammary gland (By similarity). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:P97926, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11923477, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19934046, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20647384, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21896752, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22069312, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22123970, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24367110, ECO:0000269|PubMed:32832646, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35104164, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35241813, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35851571, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6278592}.

background.label: Alzheimer Disease
background.definition: A degenerative disease of the BRAIN characterized by the insidious onset of DEMENTIA. Impairment of MEMORY, judgment, attention span, and problem solving skills are followed by severe APRAXIAS and a global loss of cognitive abilities. background.label: Cerebral Palsy
background.definition: A heterogeneous group of nonprogressive motor disorders caused by chronic brain injuries that originate in the prenatal period, perinatal period, or first few years of life. The four major subtypes are spastic, athetoid, ataxic, and mixed cerebral palsy, with spastic forms being the most common. The motor disorder may range from difficulties with fine motor control to severe spasticity (see MUSCLE SPASTICITY) in all limbs. Spastic diplegia (Little disease) is the most common subtype, and is characterized by spasticity that is more prominent in the legs than in the arms. Pathologically, this condition may be associated with LEUKOMALACIA, PERIVENTRICULAR. (From Dev Med Child Neurol 1998 Aug;40(8):520-7)

background.label: Parkinson Disease
background.definition: A progressive, degenerative neurologic disease characterized by a TREMOR that is maximal at rest, retropulsion (i.e. a tendency to fall backwards), rigidity, stooped posture, slowness of voluntary movements, and a masklike facial expression. Pathologic features include loss of melanin containing neurons in the substantia nigra and other pigmented nuclei of the brainstem. LEWY BODIES are present in the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus but may also be found in a related condition (LEWY BODY DISEASE, DIFFUSE) characterized by dementia in combination with varying degrees of parkinsonism. (Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, p1059, pp1067-75)

claims.headline: Ten-year trial links partial meniscectomy to worse outcomes than sham surgery
claims.summary: A Finnish trial followed 146 adults with meniscus tears for 10 years after assignment to partial meniscectomy or sham surgery. The surgery group had poorer knee function, greater osteoarthritis progression and a higher likelihood of later knee surgery. A surgeon said some patients with a catching sensation may still benefit, while results are less predictable when surgery is intended to relieve pain.

background.label: Parkinson Disease
background.definition: A progressive, degenerative neurologic disease characterized by a TREMOR that is maximal at rest, retropulsion (i.e. a tendency to fall backwards), rigidity, stooped posture, slowness of voluntary movements, and a masklike facial expression. Pathologic features include loss of melanin containing neurons in the substantia nigra and other pigmented nuclei of the brainstem. LEWY BODIES are present in the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus but may also be found in a related condition (LEWY BODY DISEASE, DIFFUSE) characterized by dementia in combination with varying degrees of parkinsonism. (Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, p1059, pp1067-75)

claims.headline: CDC reports that some patients experience COVID-19 symptom or test rebound after Paxlovid
claims.summary: The CDC said some people have symptoms return or test positive again two to eight days after completing Paxlovid, often improving within about three days without further treatment. It reported no severe cases identified among rebound patients. Clinical-trial results showed similar rebound rates with Paxlovid and placebo, while Paxlovid reduced hospitalization or death risk in high-risk patients.

reported_statements.text: Doctors may prescribe a longer course if signs suggest the infection is returning.

background.label: PDCD1
background.name: programmed cell death 1
background.definition: Inhibitory receptor on antigen activated T-cells that plays a critical role in induction and maintenance of immune tolerance to self (PubMed:21276005, PubMed:31754127, PubMed:32184441, PubMed:37208329). Delivers inhibitory signals upon binding to ligands CD274/PDCD1L1 and CD273/PDCD1LG2 (PubMed:21276005, PubMed:26602187). Following T-cell receptor (TCR) engagement, PDCD1 associates with TCR-CD3 in the immunological synapse and directly inhibits T-cell activation (PubMed:32184441). Suppresses T-cell activation through the recruitment of PTPN11/SHP-2: following ligand-binding, PDCD1 is phosphorylated within the ITSM motif, leading to the recruitment of the protein tyrosine phosphatase PTPN11/SHP-2 that mediates dephosphorylation of key TCR proximal signaling molecules, such as ZAP70, PRKCQ/PKCtheta and CD247/CD3zeta (PubMed:32184441). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:21276005, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26602187, ECO:0000269|PubMed:31754127, ECO:0000269|PubMed:32184441, ECO:0000269|PubMed:37208329}.

background.definition: An X-linked recessive muscle disease caused by an inability to synthesize DYSTROPHIN, which is involved with maintaining the integrity of the sarcolemma. background.label: Melanoma
background.definition: A malignant neoplasm derived from cells that are capable of forming melanin, which may occur in the skin of any part of the body, in the eye, or, rarely, in the mucous membranes of the genitalia, anus, oral cavity, or other sites. It occurs mostly in adults and may originate de novo or from a pigmented nevus or malignant lentigo. Melanomas frequently metastasize widely, and the regional lymph nodes, liver, lungs, and brain are likely to be involved. The incidence of malignant skin melanomas is rising rapidly in all parts of the world. (Stedman, 25th ed; from Rook et al., Textbook of Dermatology, 4th ed, p2445)

claims.headline: Personalized mRNA vaccine prompts immune responses in some pancreatic cancer patients
claims.summary: A small Phase 1 trial followed 16 people with early-stage pancreatic cancer who received personalized mRNA vaccines after surgery. Eight developed a T-cell response; six years later, seven responders and two nonresponders were alive. Researchers say the results suggest a possible link between vaccine response and longer survival, but note that more research is needed.

claims.headline: Light-activated therapy showed promise against glioblastoma in mice
claims.summary: A European research team tested a fluorescent dye and cancer-targeting affibody activated by near-infrared light in mice with glioblastoma. The approach helped reveal tiny tumour areas during surgery and killed remaining cells, while also prompting an immune response. Human testing is still needed, and reaching every part of a tumour with the light remains a challenge.

articles.title: Scientists harness light therapy to target and kill cancer cells in world first

background.label: Glioblastoma
background.definition: A malignant form of astrocytoma histologically characterized by pleomorphism of cells, nuclear atypia, microhemorrhage, and necrosis. They may arise in any region of the central nervous system, with a predilection for the cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia, and commissural pathways. Clinical presentation most frequently occurs in the fifth or sixth decade of life with focal neurologic signs or seizures.

organisations.name: Cancer Research UK Convergence Science Centre

reported_statements.text: The treatment made microscopic glioblastoma areas easier to see during surgery and killed cancer cells left behind when activated by near-infrared light.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: It prompted an immune response that might help the body recognise cancer cells later and could reduce the chance of glioblastoma returning.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Near-infrared light may not reach every part of a tumour, posing a technical challenge for the approach.
reported_statements.speaker: article

claims.headline: Study reports improved near vision after twice-daily eye drops for presbyopia
claims.summary: A study of 766 people in Argentina found that most participants could read additional lines on near-vision charts after using twice-daily eye drops containing pilocarpine and diclofenac. The reported improvement lasted two years; temporary dim vision, irritation and headaches were common side effects. Researchers said the treatment may offer an alternative to glasses or surgery, while an expert called for larger, longer-term studies.

background.definition: A subclass of DIABETES MELLITUS that is not INSULIN-responsive or dependent (NIDDM). It is characterized initially by INSULIN RESISTANCE and HYPERINSULINEMIA; and eventually by GLUCOSE INTOLERANCE; HYPERGLYCEMIA; and overt diabetes. Type II diabetes mellitus is no longer considered a disease exclusively found in adults. Patients seldom develop KETOSIS but often exhibit OBESITY.

It is distinguishable from WET MACULAR DEGENERATION in that the latter involves neovascular exudates.

claims.summary: In a small study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, 14 patients took baxdrostat for 6 to 12 months. Their blood pressure stayed lower for up to two years after stopping, and just under a quarter came off all treatment with normal readings. NICE is assessing the drug.

background.label: Stargardt Disease
background.definition: A juvenile-onset macular dystrophy characterized by progressive loss of VISUAL ACUITY with normal acuity in peripheral VISUAL FIELDS. Other associated clinical features may include LIPOFUSCIN fundus autofluorescence, atrophy of the RETINAL PIGMENT EPITHELIUM, loss of color vision, PHOTOPHOBIA and PARACENTRAL SCOTOMA. Germline mutations in the ABCA4 gene have been identified in recessive and dominant diseases.

claims.headline: Guy’s Hospital reports early results from ProFocal prostate cancer pilot
claims.summary: Guy’s Hospital is piloting ProFocal laser therapy in 30 patients with localised prostate cancer. The hospital reports that, among the first 10 treated, eight had no cancer detected in the treated area and two had only a small amount remaining. The pilot will include follow-up, with an MRI at one year to assess durability.

claims.headline: Doctors report improved oxygen levels after turning some COVID-19 patients onto their stomachs
claims.summary: The article describes prone positioning for COVID-19 patients, reporting that clinicians saw oxygen levels improve in some cases. It explains a possible lung-related mechanism and notes increased sedation needs for ventilated patients. A trial was underway to test the approach in patients receiving oxygen but not mechanical ventilation.

claims.headline: PrP-targeting divalent siRNA entered a phase 1 safety study for prion disease
claims.summary: Broad Institute reported in April 2026 that a divalent small interfering RNA targeting prion-protein production was entering the PRiSM phase 1 trial. Prior mouse experiments reported lower prion-protein levels and longer survival; these findings do not establish benefit in people. The trial gives a single intrathecal dose and measures safety and biological activity. An October update added people without symptoms who carry high-risk PRNP variants. This candidate is distinct from ION717 and from the gene-editing approaches also mentioned in the report.

background.label: Alcoholism
background.definition: A primary, chronic disease with genetic, psychosocial, and environmental factors influencing its development and manifestations. The disease is often progressive and fatal. It is characterized by impaired control over drinking, preoccupation with the drug alcohol, use of alcohol despite adverse consequences, and distortions in thinking, most notably denial. Each of these symptoms may be continuous or periodic. (Morse & Flavin for the Joint Commission of the National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence and the American Society of Addiction Medicine to Study the Definition and Criteria for the Diagnosis of Alcoholism: in JAMA 1992;268:1012-4)

claims.headline: FDA grants breakthrough designation to single-dose psilocybin research for major depression
claims.summary: The FDA granted the Usona Institute’s Phase 2 trial of a single psilocybin dose for major depressive disorder Breakthrough Therapy designation. The seven-site US trial planned to enroll 80 participants and compare psilocybin with niacin, alongside psychotherapy sessions. The article reports that Usona expected the trial to finish by early 2021, with Phase 3 trials possible if results were positive.

background.label: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
background.definition: An anxiety disorder characterized by recurrent, persistent obsessions or compulsions. Obsessions are the intrusive ideas, thoughts, or images that are experienced as senseless or repugnant. Compulsions are repetitive and seemingly purposeful behavior which the individual generally recognizes as senseless and from which the individual does not derive pleasure although it may provide a release from tension.

background.label: Psilocybin
background.definition: The major of two hallucinogenic components of the sacred Teonanacatl mushrooms (see PSILOCYBE), the other component being PSILOCIN.

background.label: HTR2A
background.name: 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 2A
background.definition: G protein-coupled receptor for 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin) (PubMed:1330647, PubMed:18703043, PubMed:19057895, PubMed:21645528, PubMed:22300836, PubMed:35084960, PubMed:38552625). Also functions as a receptor for various drugs and psychoactive substances, including mescaline, psilocybin, 1-(2,5-dimethoxy-4- iodophenyl)-2-aminopropane (DOI) and lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) (PubMed:28129538, PubMed:35084960). Ligand binding causes a conformation change that triggers signaling via guanine nucleotide- binding proteins (G proteins) and modulates the activity of downstream effectors (PubMed:28129538, PubMed:35084960). HTR2A is coupled to G(q)/G(11) G alpha proteins and activates phospholipase C-beta, releasing diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) second messengers that modulate the activity of phosphatidylinositol 3- kinase and promote the release of Ca(2+) ions from intracellular stores, respectively (PubMed:18703043, PubMed:28129538, PubMed:35084960). Beta-arrestin family members inhibit signaling via G proteins and mediate activation of alternative signaling pathways (PubMed:28129538, PubMed:35084960). Affects neural activity, perception, cognition and mood (PubMed:18297054). Plays a role in the regulation of behavior, including responses to anxiogenic situations and psychoactive substances. Plays a role in intestinal smooth muscle contraction, and may play a role in arterial vasoconstriction (By similarity). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:P35363, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1330647, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18297054, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18703043, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19057895, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21645528, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22300836, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28129538, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35084960, ECO:0000269|PubMed:38552625}.

background.label: HTR2A
background.name: 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor 2A
background.definition: G protein-coupled receptor for 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin) (PubMed:1330647, PubMed:18703043, PubMed:19057895, PubMed:21645528, PubMed:22300836, PubMed:35084960, PubMed:38552625). Also functions as a receptor for various drugs and psychoactive substances, including mescaline, psilocybin, 1-(2,5-dimethoxy-4- iodophenyl)-2-aminopropane (DOI) and lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) (PubMed:28129538, PubMed:35084960). Ligand binding causes a conformation change that triggers signaling via guanine nucleotide- binding proteins (G proteins) and modulates the activity of downstream effectors (PubMed:28129538, PubMed:35084960). HTR2A is coupled to G(q)/G(11) G alpha proteins and activates phospholipase C-beta, releasing diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) second messengers that modulate the activity of phosphatidylinositol 3- kinase and promote the release of Ca(2+) ions from intracellular stores, respectively (PubMed:18703043, PubMed:28129538, PubMed:35084960). Beta-arrestin family members inhibit signaling via G proteins and mediate activation of alternative signaling pathways (PubMed:28129538, PubMed:35084960). Affects neural activity, perception, cognition and mood (PubMed:18297054). Plays a role in the regulation of behavior, including responses to anxiogenic situations and psychoactive substances. Plays a role in intestinal smooth muscle contraction, and may play a role in arterial vasoconstriction (By similarity). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:P35363, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1330647, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18297054, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18703043, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19057895, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21645528, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22300836, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28129538, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35084960, ECO:0000269|PubMed:38552625}.

claims.summary: In the phase 1/2a BLUESTAR study, puxitatug samrotecan produced a 47.1% confirmed response rate in B7-H4-positive recurrent or progressive endometrial cancer at 2.4 mg/kg; the rate was 60.6% among patients previously treated with platinum and anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy. The same dose had a 24.4% response rate in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer. Nausea and blood-cell toxicities were common. Further phase 3 and combination studies are underway.

claims.headline: FDA approves Sanofi’s Qfitlia for hemophilia A and B

background.label: Malaria
background.definition: A protozoan disease caused in humans by four species of the PLASMODIUM genus: PLASMODIUM FALCIPARUM; PLASMODIUM VIVAX; PLASMODIUM OVALE; and PLASMODIUM MALARIAE; and transmitted by the bite of an infected female mosquito of the genus ANOPHELES. Malaria is endemic in parts of Asia, Africa, Central and South America, Oceania, and certain Caribbean islands. It is characterized by extreme exhaustion associated with paroxysms of high FEVER; SWEATING; shaking CHILLS; and ANEMIA. Malaria in ANIMALS is caused by other species of plasmodia.

claims.headline: Radiation plus forskolin extended survival in mouse glioblastoma models
claims.summary: A study reported that adding forskolin to radiation therapy slowed glioblastoma growth in mice and increased median survival compared with radiation alone. Some mice had long-term tumor control, while others experienced recurrence. The researchers propose that forskolin helps guide radiation-affected cancer cells into less harmful, non-dividing cell types.

background.label: Glioblastoma
background.definition: A malignant form of astrocytoma histologically characterized by pleomorphism of cells, nuclear atypia, microhemorrhage, and necrosis. They may arise in any region of the central nervous system, with a predilection for the cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia, and commissural pathways. Clinical presentation most frequently occurs in the fifth or sixth decade of life with focal neurologic signs or seizures.

background.label: Ranitidine
background.definition: A non-imidazole blocker of those histamine receptors that mediate gastric secretion (H2 receptors). It is used to treat gastrointestinal ulcers.

background.label: HRH2
background.name: histamine receptor H2
background.definition: G protein-coupled receptor for histamine, primarily mediating gastric acid secretion. Predominantly expressed in the gastric mucosa, couples to G(s) G alpha proteins upon histamine binding, leading to activation of adenylate cyclase and increased intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) levels (PubMed:38647423, PubMed:39333117). This signaling cascade stimulates parietal cells to secrete hydrochloric acid, playing a key role in digestive physiology. Also expressed in other tissues, including the heart and central nervous system, where it may contribute to cardiac stimulation and modulate neurotransmitter release (By similarity). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:P97292, ECO:0000269|PubMed:38647423, ECO:0000269|PubMed:39333117}.

background.label: SMN2
background.name: survival of motor neuron 2, centromeric
background.definition: The SMN complex catalyzes the assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs), the building blocks of the spliceosome, and thereby plays an important role in the splicing of cellular pre- mRNAs (PubMed:18984161, PubMed:9845364). Most spliceosomal snRNPs contain a common set of Sm proteins SNRPB, SNRPD1, SNRPD2, SNRPD3, SNRPE, SNRPF and SNRPG that assemble in a heptameric protein ring on the Sm site of the small nuclear RNA to form the core snRNP (Sm core) (PubMed:18984161). In the cytosol, the Sm proteins SNRPD1, SNRPD2, SNRPE, SNRPF and SNRPG are trapped in an inactive 6S pICln-Sm complex by the chaperone CLNS1A that controls the assembly of the core snRNP (PubMed:18984161). To assemble core snRNPs, the SMN complex accepts the trapped 5Sm proteins from CLNS1A forming an intermediate (PubMed:18984161). Within the SMN complex, SMN1 acts as a structural backbone and together with GEMIN2 it gathers the Sm complex subunits (PubMed:17178713, PubMed:21816274, PubMed:22101937). Binding of snRNA inside 5Sm ultimately triggers eviction of the SMN complex, thereby allowing binding of SNRPD3 and SNRPB to complete assembly of the core snRNP (PubMed:31799625). Ensures the correct splicing of U12 intron- containing genes that may be important for normal motor and proprioceptive neurons development (PubMed:23063131). Also required for resolving RNA-DNA hybrids created by RNA polymerase II, that form R- loop in transcription terminal regions, an important step in proper transcription termination (PubMed:26700805). May also play a role in the metabolism of small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNPs). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17178713, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18984161, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21816274, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22101937, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23063131, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26700805, ECO:0000269|PubMed:31799625, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9845364}.

background.label: Malaria
background.definition: A protozoan disease caused in humans by four species of the PLASMODIUM genus: PLASMODIUM FALCIPARUM; PLASMODIUM VIVAX; PLASMODIUM OVALE; and PLASMODIUM MALARIAE; and transmitted by the bite of an infected female mosquito of the genus ANOPHELES. Malaria is endemic in parts of Asia, Africa, Central and South America, Oceania, and certain Caribbean islands. It is characterized by extreme exhaustion associated with paroxysms of high FEVER; SWEATING; shaking CHILLS; and ANEMIA. Malaria in ANIMALS is caused by other species of plasmodia.

background.label: Alcoholism
background.definition: A primary, chronic disease with genetic, psychosocial, and environmental factors influencing its development and manifestations. The disease is often progressive and fatal. It is characterized by impaired control over drinking, preoccupation with the drug alcohol, use of alcohol despite adverse consequences, and distortions in thinking, most notably denial. Each of these symptoms may be continuous or periodic. (Morse & Flavin for the Joint Commission of the National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence and the American Society of Addiction Medicine to Study the Definition and Criteria for the Diagnosis of Alcoholism: in JAMA 1992;268:1012-4)

background.label: Semaglutide
background.definition: A glucagon-like peptide and GLP-1 agonist used to enhance glycemic control of TYPE 2 DIABETES MELLITUS, and for OBESITY MANAGEMENT.

background.label: GLP1R
background.name: glucagon like peptide 1 receptor
background.definition: G protein-coupled receptor for glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP- 1) (PubMed:19861722, PubMed:26308095, PubMed:27196125, PubMed:28514449, PubMed:7517895, PubMed:8216285, PubMed:8405712). Ligand binding triggers activation of a signaling cascade that leads to the activation of adenylyl cyclase and increased intracellular cAMP levels (PubMed:19861722, PubMed:26308095, PubMed:27196125, PubMed:28514449, PubMed:7517895, PubMed:8216285, PubMed:8405712). Plays a role in regulating insulin secretion in response to GLP-1 (By similarity). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:O35659, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19861722, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26308095, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27196125, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28514449, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7517895, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8216285, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8405712}.

claims.headline: Semaglutide use associated with lower Alzheimer’s risk in people with Type 2 diabetes
claims.summary: A study using medical records from more than 1 million adults with Type 2 diabetes found lower Alzheimer’s disease risk among those prescribed semaglutide than among people prescribed seven other diabetes drugs. The largest difference was versus insulin. The article says the findings do not establish whether semaglutide can prevent or treat Alzheimer’s; phase 3 trial results are expected next year.

claims.headline: A three-drug obesity combination showed lean-mass preservation with more treatment discontinuations
claims.summary: The June 2025 interim COURAGE report described semaglutide with trevogrumab and garetosmab in adults with obesity without diabetes. Compared with semaglutide alone, this three-drug regimen showed greater fat loss and less lean-mass loss, but more severe adverse events and treatment discontinuations. The interim analysis covered half the participants reaching 26 weeks; it did not establish long-term benefit.

background.label: SETD3
background.name: SET domain containing 3, actin N3(tau)-histidine methyltransferase
background.definition: Protein-histidine N-methyltransferase that specifically mediates 3-methylhistidine (tele-methylhistidine) methylation of actin at 'His-73' (PubMed:30526847, PubMed:30626964, PubMed:30785395, PubMed:31388018, PubMed:31993215). Histidine methylation of actin is required for smooth muscle contraction of the laboring uterus during delivery (PubMed:30626964). Does not have protein-lysine N- methyltransferase activity and probably only catalyzes histidine methylation of actin (PubMed:30626964, PubMed:30785395, PubMed:31388018). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:30526847, ECO:0000269|PubMed:30626964, ECO:0000269|PubMed:30785395, ECO:0000269|PubMed:31388018, ECO:0000269|PubMed:31993215}.

background.definition: A degenerative disease of the BRAIN characterized by the insidious onset of DEMENTIA. Impairment of MEMORY, judgment, attention span, and problem solving skills are followed by severe APRAXIAS and a global loss of cognitive abilities. The condition primarily occurs after age 60, and is marked pathologically by severe cortical atrophy and the triad of SENILE PLAQUES; NEUROFIBRILLARY TANGLES; and NEUROPIL THREADS. (From Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, pp1049-57)

background.label: APP
background.name: amyloid beta precursor protein
background.definition: Functions as a cell surface receptor and performs physiological functions on the surface of neurons relevant to neurite growth, neuronal adhesion and axonogenesis. Interaction between APP molecules on neighboring cells promotes synaptogenesis (PubMed:25122912). Involved in cell mobility and transcription regulation through protein-protein interactions. Can promote transcription activation through binding to APBB1-KAT5 and inhibits Notch signaling through interaction with Numb. Couples to apoptosis- inducing pathways such as those mediated by G(o) and JIP. Inhibits G(o) alpha ATPase activity (By similarity). Acts as a kinesin I membrane receptor, mediating the axonal transport of beta-secretase and presenilin 1 (By similarity). By acting as a kinesin I membrane receptor, plays a role in axonal anterograde transport of cargo towards synapses in axons (PubMed:17062754, PubMed:23011729). Involved in copper homeostasis/oxidative stress through copper ion reduction. In vitro, copper-metallated APP induces neuronal death directly or is potentiated through Cu(2+)-mediated low-density lipoprotein oxidation. Can regulate neurite outgrowth through binding to components of the extracellular matrix such as heparin and collagen I and IV. The splice isoforms that contain the BPTI domain possess protease inhibitor activity. Induces a AGER-dependent pathway that involves activation of p38 MAPK, resulting in internalization of amyloid-beta peptide and leading to mitochondrial dysfunction in cultured cortical neurons. Provides Cu(2+) ions for GPC1 which are required for release of nitric oxide (NO) and subsequent degradation of the heparan sulfate chains on GPC1. {ECO:0000250, ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:P12023, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17062754, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23011729, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25122912}.

background.label: Stiff-Person Syndrome
background.definition: A condition characterized by persistent spasms (SPASM) involving multiple muscles, primarily in the lower limbs and trunk. The illness tends to occur in the fourth to sixth decade of life, presenting with intermittent spasms that become continuous. Minor sensory stimuli, such as noise and light touch, precipitate severe spasms. Spasms do not occur during sleep and only rarely involve cranial muscles. Respiration may become impaired in advanced cases. (Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, p1492; Neurology 1998 Jul;51(1):85-93)

background.label: Sleep Apnea, Obstructive
background.definition: A disorder characterized by recurrent apneas during sleep despite persistent respiratory efforts. It is due to upper airway obstruction. The respiratory pauses may induce HYPERCAPNIA or HYPOXIA. Cardiac arrhythmias and elevation of systemic and pulmonary arterial pressures may occur. Frequent partial arousals occur throughout sleep, resulting in relative SLEEP DEPRIVATION and daytime tiredness. Associated conditions include OBESITY; ACROMEGALY; MYXEDEMA; micrognathia; MYOTONIC DYSTROPHY; adenotonsilar dystrophy; and NEUROMUSCULAR DISEASES. background.label: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
background.definition: A degenerative disorder affecting upper MOTOR NEURONS in the brain and lower motor neurons in the brain stem and SPINAL CORD. Disease onset is usually after the age of 50 and the process is usually fatal within 3 to 6 years. Clinical manifestations include progressive weakness, atrophy, FASCICULATION, hyperreflexia, DYSARTHRIA, dysphagia, and eventual paralysis of respiratory function. Pathologic features include the replacement of motor neurons with fibrous ASTROCYTES and atrophy of anterior SPINAL NERVE ROOTS and corticospinal tracts. (From Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, pp1089-94)

background.label: Prostheses and Implants
background.definition: Artificial substitutes for body parts, and materials inserted into tissue for functional, cosmetic, or therapeutic purposes. Prostheses can be functional, as in the case of artificial arms and legs, or cosmetic, as in the case of an artificial eye. Implants, all surgically inserted or grafted into the body, tend to be used therapeutically. IMPLANTS, EXPERIMENTAL is available for those used experimentally.

(From Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, pp1049-57)

background.label: Parkinson Disease
background.definition: A progressive, degenerative neurologic disease characterized by a TREMOR that is maximal at rest, retropulsion (i.e. a tendency to fall backwards), rigidity, stooped posture, slowness of voluntary movements, and a masklike facial expression. Pathologic features include loss of melanin containing neurons in the substantia nigra and other pigmented nuclei of the brainstem. LEWY BODIES are present in the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus but may also be found in a related condition (LEWY BODY DISEASE, DIFFUSE) characterized by dementia in combination with varying degrees of parkinsonism. (Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, p1059, pp1067-75)

background.definition: A subtype of DIABETES MELLITUS that is characterized by INSULIN deficiency. It is manifested by the sudden onset of severe HYPERGLYCEMIA, rapid progression to DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS, and DEATH unless treated with insulin. background.label: CD3E
background.name: CD3 epsilon subunit of T-cell receptor complex
background.definition: Part of the TCR-CD3 complex present on T-lymphocyte cell surface that plays an essential role in adaptive immune response (PubMed:15294938, PubMed:15546002, PubMed:2470098, PubMed:40592325, PubMed:8490660). When antigen presenting cells (APCs) activate T-cell receptor (TCR), TCR-mediated signals are transmitted across the cell membrane by the CD3 chains CD3D, CD3E, CD3G and CD247/CD3Z (PubMed:2470098, PubMed:40592325). All CD3 chains contain immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) in their cytoplasmic domain (PubMed:2470098, PubMed:40592325). Upon TCR engagement, these motifs become phosphorylated by Src family protein tyrosine kinases LCK and FYN, resulting in the activation of downstream signaling pathways (PubMed:2470098, PubMed:40592325). CD3E ITAM phosphorylation creates docking sites for the protein kinase ZAP70 leading to ZAP70 phosphorylation and its conversion into a catalytically active enzyme (By similarity). In addition of this role of signal transduction in T-cell activation, CD3E plays an essential role in correct T-cell development (By similarity). Also participates in internalization and cell surface down-regulation of TCR-CD3 complexes via endocytosis sequences present in CD3E cytosolic region (PubMed:10384095, PubMed:26507128). In addition to its role as a TCR coreceptor, it serves as a receptor for ITPRIPL1 (PubMed:38614099). Ligand recognition inhibits T-cell activation by promoting interaction with NCK1, which prevents CD3E-ZAP70 interaction and blocks the ERK- NFkB signaling cascade and calcium influx (PubMed:12110186, PubMed:38614099). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:P22646, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10384095, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12110186, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15294938, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15546002, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2470098, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26507128, ECO:0000269|PubMed:38614099, ECO:0000269|PubMed:40592325, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8490660}.

claims.headline: Trial reports tezepelumab benefits across severe asthma types
claims.summary: A phase 3 trial involving more than 1,000 people found that monthly tezepelumab injections reduced asthma attacks and improved lung function, asthma control and quality of life over a year compared with placebo. Benefits were reported across different asthma causes, including allergy status and eosinophil levels; the article also reports no significant side effects.

claims.headline: Coached exercise program linked to better outcomes after colon cancer treatment
claims.summary: In an international randomized trial of 889 patients who had completed chemotherapy for treatable colon cancer, participants assigned to a three-year coach-supported exercise program were more active and, after eight years, had fewer cancers and fewer deaths from any cause than those given an educational booklet. Exercise participants also had more muscle strains and similar problems.

claims.headline: BMJ investigation reports data concerns in studies supporting ticagrelor approval
claims.summary: A BMJ investigation reports inaccurate primary-endpoint results in two platelet studies cited by AstraZeneca and says some platelet-machine readings were missing from FDA datasets. The findings renew questions about the evidence for ticagrelor’s benefits compared with less expensive alternatives. An expert also raised concerns about platelet inhibition and possible clotting or bleeding risks.

background.label: IL6R
background.name: interleukin 6 receptor
background.definition: Part of the receptor for interleukin 6. Binds to IL6 with low affinity, but does not transduce a signal (PubMed:28265003). Signal activation necessitate an association with IL6ST. Activation leads to the regulation of the immune response, acute-phase reactions and hematopoiesis (PubMed:30995492, PubMed:31235509). The interaction with membrane-bound IL6R and IL6ST stimulates 'classic signaling', the restricted expression of the IL6R limits classic IL6 signaling to only a few tissues such as the liver and some cells of the immune system. Whereas the binding of IL6 and soluble IL6R to IL6ST stimulates 'trans- signaling'. Alternatively, 'cluster signaling' occurs when membrane- bound IL6:IL6R complexes on transmitter cells activate IL6ST receptors on neighboring receiver cells (Probable). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:28265003, ECO:0000269|PubMed:31235509, ECO:0000305|PubMed:30995492}.

background.label: Fibromyalgia
background.definition: A common nonarticular rheumatic syndrome characterized by myalgia and multiple points of focal muscle tenderness to palpation (trigger points). Muscle pain is typically aggravated by inactivity or exposure to cold. This condition is often associated with general symptoms, such as sleep disturbances, fatigue, stiffness, HEADACHES, and occasionally DEPRESSION. There is significant overlap between fibromyalgia and the chronic fatigue syndrome (FATIGUE SYNDROME, CHRONIC). Fibromyalgia may arise as a primary or secondary disease process. It is most frequent in females aged 20 to 50 years. (From Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, p1494-95)

background.label: Tourette Syndrome
background.definition: A neuropsychological disorder related to alterations in DOPAMINE metabolism and neurotransmission involving frontal-subcortical neuronal circuits. Both multiple motor and one or more vocal tics need to be present with TICS occurring many times a day, nearly daily, over a period of more than one year. The onset is before age 18 and the disturbance is not due to direct physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition. The disturbance causes marked distress or significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. (From DSM-IV, 1994; Neurol Clin 1997 May;15(2):357-79)

background.label: Electric Stimulation Therapy
background.definition: Application of electric current in treatment without the generation of perceptible heat. It includes electric stimulation of nerves or muscles, passage of current into the body, or use of interrupted current of low intensity to raise the detection threshold of the skin to pain.

claims.headline: AstraZeneca reports positive phase 3 results for tozorakimab in COPD
claims.summary: AstraZeneca said tozorakimab reduced moderate-to-severe COPD exacerbations versus placebo in the former-smoker primary populations of the Oberon and Titania trials, and reported a benefit in the broader populations as well. Detailed safety and efficacy data have not yet been released.

background.label: Intracranial Aneurysm
background.definition: Abnormal outpouching in the wall of intracranial blood vessels. Most common are the saccular (berry) aneurysms located at branch points in CIRCLE OF WILLIS at the base of the brain. Vessel rupture results in SUBARACHNOID HEMORRHAGE or INTRACRANIAL HEMORRHAGES. Giant aneurysms (>2.5 cm in diameter) may compress adjacent structures, including the OCULOMOTOR NERVE. (From Adams et al., Principles of Neurology, 6th ed, p841)

background.definition: A subclass of DIABETES MELLITUS that is not INSULIN-responsive or dependent (NIDDM). background.definition: Live microbial DIETARY SUPPLEMENTS which beneficially affect the host animal by improving its intestinal microbial balance. Antibiotics and other related compounds are not included in this definition. In humans, lactobacilli are commonly used as probiotics, either as single species or in mixed culture with other bacteria. Other genera that have been used are bifidobacteria and streptococci. (J. Nutr. 1995;125:1401-12)

claims.summary: ETH Zurich researchers reported in Science that their implant brought blood sugar back to normal in diabetic, obese mice within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, and the animals lost up to 10% of body weight over six weeks. Outside experts said safety questions come first. The team plans tests in pigs and sheep before any human trial.

background.label: Prostheses and Implants
background.definition: Artificial substitutes for body parts, and materials inserted into tissue for functional, cosmetic, or therapeutic purposes. Prostheses can be functional, as in the case of artificial arms and legs, or cosmetic, as in the case of an artificial eye. Implants, all surgically inserted or grafted into the body, tend to be used therapeutically. IMPLANTS, EXPERIMENTAL is available for those used experimentally.

background.label: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2
background.definition: A subclass of DIABETES MELLITUS that is not INSULIN-responsive or dependent (NIDDM). It is characterized initially by INSULIN RESISTANCE and HYPERINSULINEMIA; and eventually by GLUCOSE INTOLERANCE; HYPERGLYCEMIA; and overt diabetes. Type II diabetes mellitus is no longer considered a disease exclusively found in adults. Patients seldom develop KETOSIS but often exhibit OBESITY.

claims.headline: Urease-powered antimicrobial nanobots treated infected wounds in mice
claims.summary: Researchers tested silica nano- and microparticles propelled by urease and carrying antimicrobial peptides on infected mouse wounds. The particles spread across the wound and reduced bacterial counts throughout it, while peptide treatment without the particles’ fuel worked only near the application site. The researchers suggest the approach could be useful in other hard-to-reach infections.

articles.title: These Nanobots Can Swim Around a Wound and Kill Bacteria

reported_statements.text: Peptide-carrying bots reduced bacterial counts across infected mouse wounds by 100- to 1,000-fold.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Without urea fuel, the bots acted only near where they were applied, like the peptide treatment without bots.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: Urease uses urea to propel the particles, helping them move across the wound.
reported_statements.speaker: researcher

reported_statements.text: The antimicrobial peptides disrupt bacterial cell membranes.
reported_statements.speaker: article

reported_statements.text: The approach could help deliver treatments through thick fluids or to infections in biofilms.
reported_statements.speaker: researcher

claims.headline: Cohort study links vitamin D use with lower dementia incidence
claims.summary: In a prospective cohort of 12,388 adults, vitamin D supplement use was associated with a 40% lower dementia incidence over 10 years. The association was stronger among women, people with normal cognition, and APOE ε4 noncarriers. The article notes that clinical trials are needed to establish whether supplementation prevents or delays dementia.

background.definition: An infectious disease caused by a spirochete, BORRELIA BURGDORFERI, which is transmitted chiefly by Ixodes dammini (see IXODES) and pacificus ticks in the United States and Ixodes ricinis (see IXODES) in Europe. It is a disease with early and late cutaneous manifestations plus involvement of the nervous system, heart, eye, and joints in variable combinations. The disease was formerly known as Lyme arthritis and first discovered at Old Lyme, Connecticut.

background.label: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2
background.definition: A subclass of DIABETES MELLITUS that is not INSULIN-responsive or dependent (NIDDM). It is characterized initially by INSULIN RESISTANCE and HYPERINSULINEMIA; and eventually by GLUCOSE INTOLERANCE; HYPERGLYCEMIA; and overt diabetes. Type II diabetes mellitus is no longer considered a disease exclusively found in adults. Patients seldom develop KETOSIS but often exhibit OBESITY.

background.label: Prostheses and Implants
background.definition: Artificial substitutes for body parts, and materials inserted into tissue for functional, cosmetic, or therapeutic purposes. Prostheses can be functional, as in the case of artificial arms and legs, or cosmetic, as in the case of an artificial eye. Implants, all surgically inserted or grafted into the body, tend to be used therapeutically. IMPLANTS, EXPERIMENTAL is available for those used experimentally.

claims.headline: Experimental dissolving pacemaker is designed for temporary heartbeat support
claims.summary: Researchers developed a tiny, wireless pacemaker that can be injected, controlled by light and designed to dissolve in the body. It has been tested in several animal species and in human heart tissue in a lab, but has not yet been tested in people; its senior author estimated human testing could begin in two to three years.

claims.headline: Wave starts Phase 2a trial of WVE-007 with tirzepatide for obesity
claims.summary: Wave Life Sciences says it has begun a placebo-controlled Phase 2a study testing two doses of WVE-007 alongside weekly tirzepatide in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes. background.label: IL6
background.name: interleukin 6
background.definition: Cytokine with a wide variety of biological functions in immunity, tissue regeneration, and metabolism. Binds to IL6R, then the complex associates to the signaling subunit IL6ST/gp130 to trigger the intracellular IL6-signaling pathway (Probable). The interaction with the membrane-bound IL6R and IL6ST stimulates 'classic signaling', whereas the binding of IL6 and soluble IL6R to IL6ST stimulates 'trans- signaling'. Alternatively, 'cluster signaling' occurs when membrane- bound IL6:IL6R complexes on transmitter cells activate IL6ST receptors on neighboring receiver cells (Probable). .

claims.headline: Study links live shingles vaccine with lower cardiovascular event risk
claims.summary: A study of more than 1 million adults aged 50 and older found that recipients of a live zoster vaccine had a 23% lower risk of cardiovascular events for up to eight years. It killed carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii infections in mice and is being evaluated in Phase I human trials. The article notes that laboratory mutations reduced its effectiveness and that resistance could eventually emerge.
